notes: Literal: 'may your morning be good'. Common greeting before 10am.
Used when greeting someone in the evening. The repo's example dialogue teaches this as the evening counterpart to 'Mola'a ma'a'.
Used when parting for the day, not expecting to see the person again soon.
Used when you expect to see the person again the same day. Tone falls on 'nnu'.
Encouraging correction phrase — used by teachers/elders when a learner is close to right.
